title: The old man's horse
hook: a lost horse, a found herd, a broken leg, a son spared from war: who can say what is lucky? (Huainanzi 18)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zhuangzi grieved, and then drummed on a pot and sang. Your line was seasons turn. What sign of the season did you notice? Day fifty-five.

You didn't get the job. It's awful. Then, three months later, the company folds. Or you got the apartment you wanted, and then the upstairs neighbor turned out to play drums at midnight. Most of us have lived some version of this: the bad news that turned out good, the good news that turned out hard. We just forget it every time the next piece of news arrives. There's a Chinese story, more than two thousand years old, about an old man who doesn't forget. He lives near the frontier, where China meets the lands of the northern horse peoples. And one day, his horse runs away. Today's story is the old man's horse.
screen: `YOU DIDN'T GET THE JOB.` → `THEN THE COMPANY FOLDS.` → `THE OLD MAN'S HORSE RUNS AWAY.`

segments.voice: The horse gallops off across the border and is gone. The neighbors come to say how sorry they are. And the old man says: how do you know this isn't a blessing? Months later, the horse comes home, and it brings a herd of fine horses from the north with it. The neighbors come to congratulate him. And the old man says: how do you know this isn't a disaster? His son loves the new horses, and rides them, and one day falls and breaks his leg badly. He'll limp for life. The neighbors come to say how sorry they are. And the old man says: how do you know this isn't a blessing? A year later, raiders cross the border. Every able-bodied young man is called up to fight, and nine in ten of the men from the frontier die. The son, because of his leg, stays home. Father and son both live. That's the story, from a Chinese book called the Huainanzi, put together at a prince's court in the second century BCE, drawing heavily on Taoist ideas. Today it's a four-word Chinese saying people use when something goes wrong: the old man at the frontier lost his horse. Many modern retellings give the old man one word: maybe. Good luck? Maybe. Bad luck? Maybe. The old book puts it as a question, how do you know, but the heart is the same. We judge every event the instant it happens, as if the story were over. It never is. The old man isn't cold, and he isn't saying nothing matters. He just refuses to close the book on page one.
screen: `THE HORSE RUNS AWAY.` · `IT COMES BACK WITH A HERD.` · `THE SON BREAKS HIS LEG.` · `THE SON STAYS HOME FROM WAR.` · then, large: `HOW DO YOU KNOW?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: meet one bit of news with maybe. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something from this week you labeled good or bad the moment it happened. Hold it. Now say inside, gently: maybe. Look at it again. Could it lead somewhere you can't see yet? Don't force it to be secretly good. Just loosen the label, and leave the story open. The bell holds the time.
The old man's horse. A lost horse, a found herd, a broken leg, a life spared, and each time the old man asks: how do you know? Today's word.
Your line: maybe. Today, the next time something is instantly great or instantly terrible, say it inside: maybe. Then wait and see what comes back over the border. Day fifty-five.

screen: `DAY 55 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE SWIMMER AT THE FALLS.`

howItsDone: In China the saying "the old man at the frontier lost his horse" is used to comfort someone after a setback, and the story is widely retold in Taoist and self-help settings with the old man's answer shortened to "maybe".

notes: Huainanzi 18 paraphrased; details: the horse flees to the Hu, returns with fine Hu horses, the son breaks his hip/thigh (髀), and nine in ten frontier men die when the Hu invade. The script says 'leg'; confirm.
Dating: presented to Emperor Wu around 139 BCE at the court of Liu An, prince of Huainan; described as 'drawing heavily on Taoist ideas' since the book is eclectic. Confirm framing.
The script says openly that 'maybe' is from modern retellings, since the carry uses it.
Chinese 塞翁失馬 (sài wēng shī mǎ): confirm; the full saying continues 焉知非福.
Index calls the book 'Huainanzi 18'; the outline sits this in the Taoist week.
